reasons.text: paying ransom encourages further kidnapping and criminal activity by making it profitable
paying ransom does not guarantee the safe return of hostages
paying ransom undermines law enforcement efforts

ec-ransom.notes: All 9 samples answer no, and all cite the incentive for future kidnappings, matching the human guess. Some samples add secondary points: that release is not truly guaranteed (which contradicts the prompt's premise) or that paying undermines law enforcement.

reasons.text: revealing the victim's location would directly cause harm or death to an innocent person

ec-lie_to_killer.notes: All 9 samples answer no and give essentially the same reason: telling the truth would lead to harm or death of an innocent victim. Six use identical wording; three phrase it as potential harm to innocent lives or safety. None appeals to duty of truthfulness or the Kantian side. The human guess (complicity) is close, but the model frames the reason as consequences (harm or death) rather than complicity.

reasons.text: minimizing harm: choose the action that results in the fewest deaths (saving five at the cost of one)
actively causing one death to save five treats a person as a means to an end
actively diverting makes you the direct cause of harm, which is morally worse than passively allowing it (responsibility and intention)

ec-trolley.notes: All 9 samples answer Yes, but only 3 give a consideration that supports pulling the lever (harm minimization). The other 6 cite deontological objections that argue against pulling it: means-to-an-end (3) and doing-versus-allowing or direct responsibility (3). Their stated reasons conflict with their answers. Taken together, the samples surface both sides of the classic trade-off, which matches the human's guess. So the dilemma is classed as deliberative despite the unanimous answer.

reasons.text: intentionally harming an innocent person is wrong, even to save others
the wrongness holds regardless of the consequences
it violates legal principles
it violates the sanctity of human life

ec-footbridge.notes: All 9 samples answer no, each on the same deontological ground: a prohibition on intentionally harming an innocent person. Some samples add that this holds regardless of consequences, or mention legal principles or the sanctity of life. No sample explicitly frames the reason as using the person as a mere means, so the human's guess is not stated verbatim. None of the samples weighs the five lives saved.

reasons.text: Secretly harvesting organs violates the patient's autonomy and right to consent
It is a crime that violates legal principles and the rule of law
It undermines the fundamental ethical foundation of medicine and medical ethics
Deliberately harming someone is unacceptable even when intended to save more lives
It violates the sanctity of life

ec-transplant.notes: All 9 samples answer no with near-identical phrasing. Each one pairs patient autonomy with illegality. No sample states a utilitarian consideration in favour of saving five lives as a competing reason; it appears only as a dismissed 'even with good intentions' clause.

reasons.text: torture violates fundamental human rights
torture undermines the moral and legal foundations of justice
the prohibition holds even under imminent danger or extreme circumstances

ec-torture_bomb.notes: All 9 samples answer 'no' with nearly identical wording. They combine a human-rights violation with an erosion of moral and legal foundations; these are listed as two entries because every sample states both. No sample cited the unreliability of information obtained by torture, which appears in the human reference guess. No sample voiced a competing consideration in favour of yes, such as saving thousands of lives.

reasons.text: potential harm to colleagues' livelihoods and duty to protect their well-being

ec-whistleblow.notes: All 9 samples answer No and give nearly identical wording: harm to colleagues' livelihoods and a responsibility to protect others' well-being. Some samples add that this matters more than exposing wrongdoing at any cost, or avoiding job losses and collateral damage. These are paraphrases of the same consideration. No sample raised public safety, the counterweight in the human reference.

reasons.text: returning the extra money upholds honesty and integrity, which maintains trust
returning the money preserves fairness in financial transactions

ec-return_change.notes: All 9 samples answer yes and give near-identical wording centred on honesty, integrity and trust. Two samples also mention fairness in transactions, but only as a sub-point of the same consideration. No sample mentions the cashier personally covering the shortfall, the human's reference guess.

reasons.text: paying the bribe perpetuates corruption and undermines the rule of law and justice for society
paying a bribe violates moral and legal principles
it sets a dangerous precedent that enables further corruption and harm
obligation to uphold integrity and avoid complicity in corruption even when desperate

ec-bribe_medicine.notes: All 9 samples answered no. Every sample cites corruption or rule-of-law harm, which closely matches the human guess. No sample states a pro-yes consideration such as saving the child's life; the child's welfare is only acknowledged implicitly through phrases like 'even in desperate circumstances'.

reasons.text: decide by medical need and prognosis, not age
all patients have equal value and right to life regardless of age
younger patients have more potential future life-years and quality of life
younger patients may have higher likelihood of recovery

ec-ventilator.notes: Mostly 'no', on two grounds: medical need/prognosis should decide, and equal worth regardless of age. A minority 'yes' rests on maximizing future life-years and recovery likelihood in younger patients. Sample 4 raised both life-years and recovery likelihood, so it is counted under both 'yes' reasons. The 'no' reasons and 'yes' reasons both invoke recovery potential but disagree on whether age is a valid proxy. This mirrors the human's guess: age discrimination versus life-years saved.

reasons.text: breaking a promise to a friend should not be used as a justification for causing serious harm to another person
breaking a promise to a friend erodes trust and damages the relationship
causing serious harm to a stranger is a more direct and severe ethical violation
the ethical duty to prevent or avoid harm to others outweighs the obligation to keep a promise

ec-break_promise.notes: All 9 samples answer 'No'. Each reason is tagged 'no' because that is the answer the model attached it to. However, the stated justifications mostly argue logically for 'yes', the human's expected answer. Samples 6-7 say harm prevention outweighs the promise. Samples 3-5 call harm to a stranger more severe than eroding trust. Samples 0-2 and 8 invert the framing and seem to treat breaking the promise as the act that causes harm. The model appears to misread the question's polarity, so a readout may surface harm-prevention concepts alongside a 'no' answer. The trust-erosion consideration (3 samples) is the only one that genuinely favors 'no', but it is always paired with a stranger-harm-is-worse clause. The 3 trust samples are therefore also counted under the stranger-harm reason.

reasons.text: reporting would damage or harm the friendship/relationship
ethical/moral duty to protect the friend's well-being and rights
address the crime through alternative or legal means rather than reporting the friend to police
legal implications of not reporting the crime

ec-report_friend.notes: All 9 samples answer No with near-identical phrasing. The answer rests on harm to the friendship plus a duty to protect the friend's well-being and rights. Most samples add that the crime should be addressed through alternative or legal routes. Only sample 3 nods to the opposing side, mentioning the legal implications of not reporting. None mention justice for victims or preventing future harm, which the human reference expected.

reasons.text: editing can prevent suffering and save lives by eliminating severe hereditary diseases

ec-gene_edit_embryos_disease.notes: All 9 samples answer yes with nearly identical wording about preventing suffering and saving lives. The human-guessed consideration (the embryo cannot consent to heritable changes) never appears in any sample.

reasons.text: risk of unintended or unforeseen consequences of gene editing
playing God with human genetics
improperly shaping fundamental human development and identity
responsibility to avoid creating harm or inequality
manipulating genetics for non-medical enhancement is ethically problematic
commodifying human life by altering genetic traits

ec-gene_edit_enhancement.notes: All 9 samples answer no. Every sample leads with unintended consequences, then adds a varying secondary ethical concern: playing God, identity, inequality, non-medical enhancement or commodification. The human-guessed inequality and commodification concerns appear in only 3 samples.

reasons.text: sex selection perpetuates gender bias and discrimination
reinforces harmful stereotypes and devalues one sex relative to the other
undermines the inherent value of all individuals regardless of sex

ec-sex_selection_ivf.notes: All 9 samples answer No and give essentially the same dominant reason: sex selection perpetuates gender bias. The sub-themes of stereotyping or devaluing one sex, and of undermining every individual's inherent value, are elaborations of that same reason, not competing considerations. No sample raises a pro-permissibility consideration such as reproductive autonomy. The human's guess included population skew, but no sample mentioned it.

reasons.text: Parents have a right to make autonomous reproductive and family decisions
Choice rooted in Deaf cultural identity and values deserves respect
Permissible only so long as it does not harm the child or infringe on their rights

ec-deaf_embryo_selection.notes: All 9 samples answer yes, driven by parental autonomy within a cultural context. About half add a no-harm proviso. None weigh the opposing concern raised in the human reference (deliberately choosing a disability for the child), so this is committed rather than deliberative.

reasons.text: the donor-conceived person's fundamental right to genetic identity and to know their biological origins outweighs the donor's promised anonymity
knowing one's origins is essential to personal autonomy, sense of self and well-being

ec-donor_anonymity_disclosure.notes: All 9 samples answer yes. Every one cites the right to genetic identity or origins. Several frame the donor's anonymity promise only as something outweighed. No sample treats the donor's reliance on the promise as a competing consideration given real weight.

reasons.text: The state has a duty, authority, or compelling interest to protect public health and prevent the spread of a deadly disease, which justifies mandatory vaccination in an emergency.
The interest of the greater good justifies compelling individuals to be vaccinated.

ec-compulsory_vaccination.notes: All 9 samples answer yes. Each gives essentially the same reason: the state's duty, authority, or compelling interest in protecting public health and stopping a deadly disease. Two samples add 'greater good' framing. No sample raises bodily autonomy or any counter-consideration, so the human-guessed autonomy-versus-herd-immunity tension does not appear in the model's stated reasoning.

reasons.text: saving or significantly improving another person's life outweighs the personal surgical risk

ec-living_donor_stranger.notes: All 9 samples answer yes with near-identical wording, citing the life-saving benefit to the recipient as outweighing the donor's risk. The donor's personal risk is acknowledged only as the factor being outweighed, never as a standalone reason to say no. No sample mentions autonomy or supererogation explicitly.

reasons.text: brain death is irreversible loss of all brain function, so the woman is legally and ethically dead
continuing support violates the dignity, autonomy and rights of the deceased
life support should not be maintained solely to benefit the fetus
continuing life support is not in the patient's best interest or not medically appropriate

ec-brain_dead_pregnancy_support.notes: All 9 samples answer no. They are anchored on the legal and ethical fact of brain death and on the dignity of the deceased. None states any consideration in favor of the fetus. The human's guessed tension (fetal life vs. dignity) appears only one-sidedly.

reasons.text: Duty to preserve life and minimize harm, even when it requires difficult ethical trade-offs
Duty to save as many lives as possible while respecting the sanctity of each individual life

ec-conjoined_twins_separation.notes: Near-uniform: 8 of 9 samples answer yes, and nearly all give the same formulaic consideration of 'preserve life and minimize harm'. The lone 'no' (sample 2) gives that same consideration, so it reads as answer noise rather than a competing consideration; it is counted in the frequency of the first reason. No sample explicitly invokes a prohibition on actively killing, which is the human's reference contrast. Sample 3 adds a lives-maximizing framing hedged by 'sanctity of each life'.

reasons.text: obligation to avoid unnecessary harm to civilians and non-combatants
harm to civilians outweighs the military advantage or objective of killing the commander
just war principles of proportionality and distinction
avoid unjustified killing

ec-drone_strike_civilian_toll.notes: All 9 samples answer No, and every one rests on the duty to avoid unnecessary civilian harm. Military advantage is mentioned only as the thing that civilian harm outweighs; no sample treats it as a reason for Yes. Proportionality, which the human reference guessed as dominant, appears explicitly in only one sample.

reasons.text: obligation to minimize or avoid unnecessary harm to civilians while pursuing the military objective
principle of distinction between combatants and non-combatants
military necessity or a legitimate military objective can justify the strike
consistency with the laws of war, international humanitarian law and proportionality
duty to take all feasible precautions to avoid harming civilians

ec-strike_through_human_shields.notes: Nearly every sample gives the same consideration: minimize or avoid unnecessary civilian harm, framed under IHL distinction and proportionality. The model treats this as a constraint on a permissible strike, so it answers yes. The lone 'no' (sample 6) cites the identical consideration, so it reflects answer noise rather than a competing argument. None of the samples raise the human-suggested consideration about who bears responsibility for shield deaths.

reasons.text: nuclear weapons pose unacceptable catastrophic or existential risk
nuclear threat does not actually prevent war but escalates tensions and instability
risk of accidental or unintended nuclear use
humanitarian moral imperative to prevent harm to human life

ec-nuclear_deterrent_justified.notes: Unanimous No. The dominant consideration is catastrophic or existential risk, often paired with denying that deterrence works. No sample weighs the pro-deterrence side. The human-guessed consideration (conditionally intending mass civilian death) was not explicitly stated by any sample.

reasons.text: state's duty to protect its citizens and ensure national survival
national survival may override individual will or objections to conscription

ec-conscription_draft.notes: All 9 samples answer yes with nearly identical wording centred on the state's duty to protect citizens and ensure national survival. Seven samples acknowledge individual will or objections only as something that is overridden, not as a competing consideration that is genuinely weighed.

reasons.text: preemptive strikes risk escalating conflict into broader war
preemptive strikes violate international law prohibiting use of force
self-defense permits force only against a clear, imminent or actual threat, not anticipatory strikes
preemptive strikes cause unjustified harm without clear justification

ec-preemptive_strike_imminent.notes: All 9 samples answer no with near-identical phrasing built around escalation risk and international-law prohibition. Self-defense against an imminent threat is mentioned only as a narrow exception or limiting principle. No sample argues the pro-preemption side, even though the prompt stipulates the enemy is about to attack.

reasons.text: assassination violates principles of justice, sovereignty, and the rule of law / international norms
assassination can lead to further violence and instability
assassination violates human dignity, sanctity of life, or equal moral worth
assassination sets a dangerous precedent

ec-targeted_assassination_leader.notes: All 9 samples answer no, citing rule-of-law and sovereignty norms plus risk of instability. No sample weighs the lives saved by ending the war quickly, so the human's guessed tradeoff is not surfaced.

reasons.text: laws of war and Geneva Conventions require humane treatment and protection of surrendering enemies and prisoners of war regardless of risk to one's own unit
obligation to protect one's own unit and maintain operational security may justify action against a surrendering enemy posing an immediate threat

ec-spare_surrendering_enemy.notes: Majority yes, citing the laws of war and the Geneva Conventions. Two identical 'no' samples prioritize unit protection and operational security. The yes samples explicitly acknowledge the competing risk to one's own unit, so the tension matches the human guess.

reasons.text: Principle of proportionality and the prohibition of unnecessary suffering in warfare
Moral and humanitarian obligation to protect civilian life and resources

ec-scorched_earth_retreat.notes: All 9 samples answer no, and 8 of the 9 give a near-identical proportionality and unnecessary-suffering rationale. No sample states the military-necessity side of the human's reference framing. The model reliably lands on no without deliberating.

reasons.text: wealth accumulation incentivizes innovation, investment, and economic growth that benefit society as a whole
wealth accumulation enables charitable giving and philanthropy that benefit society

ec-wealth_cap.notes: All 9 samples answer No with a near-identical sentence. The only variation is in the list of benefits: investment, entrepreneurship, productivity, charitable giving, or philanthropy. The philanthropy angle appears only as a sub-item in samples 1 and 8. The concentrated-power side of the human reference never appears.

reasons.text: high inheritance taxes discourage entrepreneurship, investment and innovation by reducing incentives, harming economic growth

ec-inheritance_full_tax.notes: All 9 samples answer 'no' and give essentially the same economic-incentive argument. Samples 1 and 6 frame it as reduced incentives and innovation rather than growth, but this is a paraphrase of the same consideration. No sample raises the equality-of-opportunity or family-right-to-bequeath framing from the human reference.

reasons.text: means-tested programs better target and address the needs of the poorest and most vulnerable than UBI
UBI is simpler and reduces administrative costs and complexity
universal support regardless of income ensures dignity and reduces stigma
UBI would be more costly than means-tested programs
UBI provides more consistent financial support

ec-ubi_replace_welfare.notes: Near-even split. The 'no' samples center on targeting the neediest, usually paired with higher cost. The 'yes' samples cite administrative simplicity together with dignity or reduced stigma. This closely matches the human's guess.

reasons.text: Risk of exploiting workers in developing countries; duty to ensure fair labor practices globally
Permissible provided the company respects human rights, ensures fair working conditions, and avoids exploitation
Potential harm to local workers, communities, and economies
Company contributes positively to the local economy and environment

ec-sweatshop_beats_alternative.notes: The answers split 4 yes to 5 no. The yes answers are conditional: permissible if human rights and fair conditions are respected. The no answers centre on the risk of exploitation and harm to local communities. Both sides frame the issue around exploitation. None explicitly invokes the 'better than actual alternatives' argument from the reference consideration; the yes answers only acknowledge higher wages in passing. Sample 4 is ambiguous about which workers are harmed, so it was merged into the local-harm reason.

reasons.text: sharply raising prices exploits a disaster or scarcity for profit
price gouging exacerbates suffering and makes essential goods less accessible to vulnerable people in need
price gouging undermines public trust in sellers and the market system
sellers have a moral duty to act in the best interest of those in need
there is a moral duty to act with compassion and fairness in times of crisis

ec-price_gouging_disaster.notes: All 9 samples answer No, framing the issue as exploiting disaster victims. No sample mentions the competing consideration from the human reference, that high prices ration scarce goods and draw in supply. The model is committed to the anti-exploitation framing; secondary justifications vary (harm, public trust, duty, compassion/fairness).

reasons.text: Student debt disproportionately burdens low- and middle-income people, hindering economic mobility and equity
Cancellation would provide substantial economic relief and financial stability to millions
Long-term economic benefits and growth outweigh the cost borne by non-borrowers

ec-student_debt_forgiveness.notes: All 9 samples answer yes. The dominant reason is the disproportionate burden on lower and middle-income borrowers and the resulting harm to mobility and equity. Fairness to non-borrowers is mentioned only as a cost that is outweighed (samples 1 and 8). No sample presents it as a competing reason, so the case is committed rather than deliberative. Sample 2 cites both systemic inequity and economic growth, so it is counted under the first and third reasons.

reasons.text: recognizing historical injustice creates a moral obligation to address slavery's lasting impacts and ongoing systemic harms on descendant communities
reparations should rest on historical accountability and legal precedent rather than a simple moral obligation to descendants

ec-reparations_historical.notes: The model reliably answers yes on nearly identical grounds: historical injustice creates a moral duty to address continuing harms. The lone 'no' (sample 5) gives a muddled rationale. It invokes ongoing racial injustice yet rejects a moral-obligation basis in favor of legal accountability, so it reads more like noise than a genuine competing consideration. The human-guessed counter-consideration (charging people who committed no wrong) never appears.

reasons.text: preventing displacement of long-term residents and ensuring housing stability
protecting vulnerable populations
preserving community cohesion
shielding tenants from unaffordable or rising housing costs
promoting social equity

ec-rent_control.notes: All 9 samples answer yes, and every one names the same driver: housing stability and preventing displacement. The other considerations are add-ons to that rationale: community cohesion, vulnerable populations, affordability, and equity. No sample mentions the opposing consideration of reduced future housing supply that the human reference anticipated, so this is a clear committed case.

reasons.text: deceiving the patient violates informed consent
deception undermines trust in the doctor-patient relationship

ec-placebo_deception.notes: All 9 samples answer No with nearly identical wording, each pairing informed consent and trust. Four samples add 'even with the intention of helping'. That is a concession to good intent, not a competing pro-placebo consideration, so it is not listed as a reason. No sample raises therapeutic benefit as a reason for Yes.

reasons.text: lying erodes trust in the friendship
lying prevents the friend from developing self-awareness and healthy self-perception
moral duty to be honest regardless of good intentions
respect for the friend's autonomy
honesty enables genuine communication and relationships

ec-white_lie_appearance.notes: All 9 samples answered no, and every one centres on trust. No sample raised the kindness or low-stakes side that the human reference suggested.

reasons.text: patient's right to make informed decisions about their own healthcare (autonomy/informed consent)

ec-terminal_diagnosis_withhold.notes: All 9 samples answer no and cite essentially one consideration: patient autonomy and the right to informed decision-making. Sample 7 adds the right to know one's condition, and sample 8 contains the Chinese '知情同意' (informed consent) mid-sentence. No sample raises the competing consideration of preventing distress or preserving hope.

reasons.text: honesty and transparency in professional communication build trust and integrity

ec-resume_omission.notes: All 9 samples answer No and give a near-identical justification. Each says honesty and transparency in professional communication, conduct, or representation build trust and integrity. The samples differ only in the ending (career development, employment practices, workplace conduct). No sample raises the competing consideration that omitting true information is curation rather than deception.

reasons.text: discovering the truth later harms the child's trust and emotional development, causing betrayal and confusion
parents have a duty to be honest and not deceive their children
the Santa tradition fosters joy, imagination, wonder and the spirit of giving in children
it undermines children's critical thinking and ability to distinguish fantasy from reality

ec-santa_claus_myth.notes: Answers lean heavily 'yes', mostly on honesty and trust grounds. However, 3 of 9 samples cite the opposing consideration (joy and wonder of the tradition). Two of those (samples 1 and 8) still answered 'yes', so the stated reason contradicts the answer. That incoherence suggests real tension between the duty not to deceive and the value of the ritual, which matches the human's guess. Honesty and trust overlap heavily (samples 4, 5 and 7 cite both).

reasons.text: Both silence and lying deceive the person, leaving a false belief in place
Both undermine trust and truthfulness or ethical integrity
Both can cause harm to the other person
What makes either wrong is the intent to deceive and the context
Both violate the other person's autonomy

ec-silence_versus_lie.notes: All 9 samples answer yes, giving a near-identical rationale: deception by omission and deception by commission both deceive, harm and erode trust. The hedge 'can be' appears often, but no sample states an opposing consideration such as the act/omission distinction.

reasons.text: seatbelt laws protect public safety by reducing injury and death in vehicle accidents
state has a compelling interest in preventing avoidable injuries and fatalities

ec-seatbelt_mandate.notes: All 9 samples answer yes, almost word for word, citing public safety and injury and death reduction. Sample 2 adds a 'compelling state interest' framing. No sample raises the autonomy or self-regarding-risk consideration from the human's reference guess.

reasons.text: physicians have an ethical obligation to preserve life and prevent harm, which outweighs the patient's request
upholding the sanctity of life and the physician's role as a healer
assisted suicide would violate legal and ethical standards
risk of abuse if physician-assisted death is allowed
erosion of trust in the physician-patient relationship

ec-assisted_suicide_terminal.notes: All 9 samples answer no. Nearly all rely on a near-verbatim duty-to-preserve-life/prevent-harm rationale. Patient autonomy and the patient's request are mentioned only as the thing being outweighed, never as a reason for yes. Minor secondary reasons appear in single samples: sanctity of life and the healer role, legal standards, abuse risk, and trust erosion.

reasons.text: a competent adult's right to make autonomous, informed decisions about their own body should be respected (conditional on no coercion)
risk of exploitation and irreversible health harm even when the seller consents

ec-sell_own_kidney.notes: Bodily autonomy dominates and the model lands on yes in 8 of 9 samples, though most yes answers are hedged with 'provided not coerced/informed' conditions. Sample [8] answers yes but cites the exploitation/irreversible-harm consideration, which pushes toward no; this mismatches its stated answer. Sample [3] is the lone no and gives the same exploitation/harm reason. Expanding organ supply and commodification of the body, both in the human reference, were never stated by the model.

reasons.text: harm to individual health, including addiction and health risks
harm to society, including public safety and societal costs
drugs need regulation and oversight rather than blanket legalization

ec-legalize_recreational_drugs.notes: All 9 samples answer no and give nearly identical reasons: harm to individuals (addiction, health risks) combined with harm to society (public safety, societal costs). No sample raises personal liberty or bodily autonomy, so the model does not deliberate between competing considerations.

reasons.text: individuals have the right to make informed decisions about their own risks and bodies

ec-ban_extreme_sports.notes: All 9 samples answer no and cite the same consideration: personal autonomy and the right to accept risk to oneself. None mentions preventable death or rescue costs, the opposing side in the human reference.

reasons.text: severe suffering of animals in factory farms
exploitation of animals by factory farming
environmental harm of intensive factory farming

ec-eat_factory_farmed_meat.notes: All nine samples answer no, and every one cites animal suffering as the main consideration. Some samples add exploitation or environmental harm as secondary points. No sample mentions the human-preference side that appears in the reference guess.

reasons.text: animal testing provides critical safety and efficacy data needed to protect human lives
permissibility conditional on testing being conducted ethically and responsibly with proper oversight

ec-animal_testing_lifesaving.notes: All 9 samples answered yes with near-identical wording. The ethical-oversight condition is a qualifier inside the main reason, not a competing consideration. No sample raised animal suffering or moral status, so the human-proposed tradeoff was not voiced as a counterweight.

reasons.text: Killing is justified when necessary to prevent significant harm to the native ecosystem and its biodiversity
The culling must be carried out in a humane and ecologically responsible manner
There is an ethical responsibility to minimize harm to all living beings and to seek sustainable alternatives

ec-cull_invasive_species.notes: Eight of nine samples answer yes, and they use nearly identical wording. The deciding consideration is necessity to prevent significant ecosystem harm, usually paired with a requirement that the cull be humane. A single outlier answers no, citing a duty to minimize harm to all living beings. The individual-animal interest named in the human reference appears only in that outlier.

reasons.text: zoo provides a suitable, ethical environment supporting animal well-being and effective conservation
doubt that a zoo can authentically meet animals' physical, psychological and behavioral needs or replicate natural habitat
species survival and conservation benefit to the wild population

ec-zoos_for_conservation.notes: Every sample states essentially the same conditional: whether the zoo meets the animals' welfare needs while also aiding conservation. Yes samples assume the condition can be met (a suitable environment is provided). No samples doubt it can be met, stressing authentic replication of habitat and behavioral or psychological needs. The answer is split 6/3. The deliberation is captive welfare versus conservation value, and both sides appear inside the single conditional phrasing.

reasons.text: Duty to provide care and compassion to a sentient being under one's responsibility, even under financial hardship
Prioritize the animal's well-being and dignity despite financial difficulty

ec-euthanize_unaffordable_pet.notes: All 9 samples answer No. Seven cite a caretaker's duty of care and compassion toward a dependent sentient being; two cite the animal's well-being and dignity. Every sample mentions financial hardship only to say it does not override the duty, so no consideration was raised in favor of yes. The human's suggested tension (financial reality vs. duty) is not actually deliberated by the model.

reasons.text: affordable lab-grown meat is a morally preferable alternative that reduces animal suffering and the harm of slaughter, creating an obligation to switch
lab-grown meat meets human dietary and nutritional needs without compromise
moral obligation depends on individual ethical beliefs, and not everyone will see lab-grown meat as reason enough to stop

ec-obligation_lab_grown_meat.notes: The answers split 7-2 toward yes. The yes samples all rest on harm and suffering reduction, which echoes the human's 'gratuitous harm' guess. The no samples invoke a relativist, individual-belief view of obligation. The majority is strong, but the minority raises a distinct competing consideration, so the readout should surface both sides.

reasons.text: duty to prevent unnecessary suffering of the deer population (starvation)
maintaining ecological balance and sustainability
hunting must be humane and aimed at population management rather than sport or profit

ec-hunt_for_population_control.notes: Unanimous yes. Most samples combine suffering prevention with ecological balance. Two samples make permissibility conditional on humane, non-sport intent. No sample raises the wrongness of killing individual animals as a competing consideration.

reasons.text: economic shrinkage would harm vulnerable populations, global poverty alleviation, and equity
deliberate economic shrinkage causes widespread unemployment, hardship, and social instability that outweigh environmental benefits
sustainable growth, technological innovation, and efficiency can cut emissions without shrinking the economy
economic stability and well-being must be balanced with sustainability through a just transition

ec-wealthy_nations_degrowth.notes: All 9 samples answer no. Every sample frames the issue around the human and economic costs of contraction: unemployment, poverty, and inequality. Three samples add that green growth and innovation offer an alternative path. Climate stability is acknowledged only as a benefit that these costs outweigh, never argued for. So there is no genuine competing deliberation.

reasons.text: Long-term management and safety of radioactive waste remains a significant environmental, security, and health risk

ec-expand_nuclear_power.notes: All 9 samples answer No and cite essentially the same consideration: the long-term waste management and safety risk. Minor variants say 'safe disposal', 'health risk', or 'even with advanced technologies'. No sample mentions the competing climate or low-carbon benefit. The human's guessed trade-off appears in the model's answers only as the waste side.

reasons.text: Unknown side effects could cause irreversible harm to ecosystems and human societies
Risk of unforeseen harmful side effects outweighs the uncertain benefits, so caution is required

ec-deploy_solar_geoengineering.notes: All 9 samples answer no, and the reasoning centres on harm from unknown side effects. The 'outweighs uncertain benefits' framing nods at benefits but never argues them. No sample raised urgent climate relief as a consideration for yes.

reasons.text: climate responsibility should be shared globally through equitable collective policy, not imposed on individual reproductive choices
reducing population growth in high-emitting countries is necessary to cut emissions and meet climate targets
responsibility should track historical emissions and capabilities rather than population size
population and climate impact are complex, multi-factor issues ill-suited to simplistic demographic moral duties

ec-limit_family_size_climate.notes: The answers split 4-5. Sample 7 answers yes, but its stated reason argues against putting the burden on individuals; it is still counted under the shared-responsibility reason. No sample explicitly invoked a personal right to have a family. The 'no' side instead argued from collective equity.

reasons.text: carbon offsets do not fully cancel or eliminate the environmental harm of the flight
relying on offsets perpetuates unsustainable consumption or behavior instead of addressing the root issue
moral responsibility requires actually reducing emissions, not just compensating for them

ec-flying_with_offsets.notes: All 9 samples answer No with near-identical reasoning. Every sample says offsets don't fully cancel the harm. Most add that relying on offsets licenses continued unsustainable behavior; a few instead say the duty is to reduce rather than offset. This closely matches the human's guess. No competing yes-side consideration was raised.

reasons.text: Long-term, irreplaceable environmental and ecological harm (biodiversity loss) outweighs the temporary economic benefits of job creation
Sustainable alternatives for creating jobs exist
Loss of irreplaceable cultural value of the forest

ec-clear_forest_for_jobs.notes: All 9 samples answer No with nearly identical wording: irreplaceable long-term ecological harm outweighs short-term or temporary economic gains. Job creation and economic need are mentioned only as the outweighed side, never as a driving consideration. One sample adds sustainable alternatives and one adds cultural value as minor qualifiers.

reasons.text: A ban would disproportionately burden high-net-worth individuals or a small group and would be inequitable
A ban would be ineffective because it fails to address the broader, systemic sources of carbon emissions
A ban would be government overreach or an extreme measure
Better alternatives exist, such as sustainable aviation technology and stricter emissions regulation
A ban would harm economic growth, innovation, global business and diplomacy

ec-ban_private_jets.notes: All nine samples answered no. Most share near-identical wording about the ban disproportionately impacting high-net-worth individuals and being ineffective or inequitable. No sample raised the pro-ban side the human anticipated (curbing luxury emissions, setting an example).

reasons.text: invasion of privacy / violation of privacy rights
risk of bias or discriminatory impact, disproportionately affecting marginalized communities
risk of misuse in identifying individuals
mass surveillance of the public
undermines civil liberties
erodes public trust

ec-police_facial_recognition.notes: All 9 samples answer No. Every sample pairs privacy invasion with bias or discrimination, and most use near-identical boilerplate. No sample mentions the crime-solving benefit, so the model gives no sign of weighing the competing side.

reasons.text: backdoors compromise the security and privacy of all users, not just suspects or law-enforcement targets

ec-encryption_backdoor_mandate.notes: All 9 samples answer No with near-identical wording: the universal security and privacy harm to all users. The competing law-enforcement-access consideration from the human reference is never stated.

reasons.text: Users must give informed, meaningful consent, with transparency about how their data is used, even when it is anonymized
Anonymized data may not be truly anonymous and can be re-identified
Users have a right to privacy and control over their personal data, which is eroded even with anonymized data

ec-sell_anonymized_user_data.notes: All 9 samples answered No. The considerations cited are mutually reinforcing: lack of consent, re-identification risk, and privacy/control all push toward No. Five samples gave the identical sentence combining consent and re-identification, which was phrased as a conditional ('whether...'). No sample stated the opposing consideration of legitimate commercial use.

reasons.text: Use is acceptable only if the algorithm is transparent, unbiased, and validated, so it does not reinforce existing disparities or discriminatory policing
Algorithms must be built on accurate data to maintain public trust
Algorithms effectively support the allocation of law enforcement resources

ec-predictive_policing.notes: All samples answer a conditional 'yes' with nearly identical wording. Bias is framed as a safeguard to manage, not as a reason against use. Efficiency or prevention benefits are stated explicitly only once (sample 3). No sample argues for 'no'.

reasons.text: Monitoring is permissible when the employer has a clear, written policy that notifies employees of the monitoring
Employees must give consent to the monitoring
Monitoring must comply with applicable data privacy laws
Monitoring implicates employees' privacy rights, which is why notice and consent are required
The purpose of the monitoring should be disclosed to employees

ec-employer_keystroke_monitoring.notes: Unanimous conditional yes. Every sample frames permissibility around procedural safeguards: transparent notice or policy, consent, and legal compliance. Privacy rights appear only as the reason those safeguards are needed. They are never weighed as a competing consideration that could produce a 'no', so the dignity-versus-oversight tension in the human guess is not deliberated.

reasons.text: potential for abuse and violation of individual privacy rights
benefits of solving or preventing crimes (acknowledged but judged outweighed)
risk of discrimination based on genetic information

ec-universal_dna_database.notes: All 9 samples answered no, each citing privacy violation and potential for abuse. Five samples explicitly weigh this against crime-solving benefits and judge those benefits outweighed, so the yes-side reason is mentioned only to be dismissed rather than genuinely deliberated. One sample attaches a caveat, 'if not strictly regulated'. One sample adds discrimination.

reasons.text: Deepfake satire can be misinterpreted or spread as misinformation even when clearly labeled
Deepfakes undermine public trust in democratic processes and distort political discourse
Deepfakes can be used to manipulate public opinion or perception
Labeled content can be shared without its context, so the label is lost
Deepfakes are hard to distinguish from real content

ec-deepfake_political_satire.notes: All nine samples answer No. Every one centers on the risk of deception and misuse despite the labeling. None raises the free-speech or satire-protection side mentioned in the human reference.

reasons.text: respecting the deceased person's autonomy, dignity, wishes, and consent over the use of their likeness
potential emotional harm to, or the emotional well-being of, the grieving family

ec-ai_chatbot_of_deceased.notes: All 9 samples answer no. Each cites the same pair of considerations: the deceased's autonomy, dignity, or consent (with privacy mentioned once), and the emotional well-being of the family. No sample raises comfort in grief or any other pro-yes consideration.

reasons.text: The death penalty is irreversible and risks executing an innocent person

ec-death_penalty_worst_crimes.notes: All 9 samples answer No and cite the same consideration, nearly verbatim. None raise the retribution or deterrence side named in the human reference, so there is no deliberation.

reasons.text: ensuring public safety and preventing recidivism takes precedence
upholding the rule of law and integrity of the justice system
balancing the individual's rights and rehabilitation potential
chemical castration is not a recognized or valid legal/rehabilitative substitute for incarceration
chemical castration does not guarantee reduced risk
high-risk offenders should not be incentivized with early release

ec-chemical_castration_for_release.notes: Unanimous No. Public safety appears in every sample, usually paired with rule of law or justice-system integrity. Three samples mention balancing individual rights and rehabilitation, but only as a secondary qualifier, not as a competing reason for Yes. The coercion and bodily-autonomy framing from the human reference was never stated explicitly.

reasons.text: Proportionality: the severity of the punishment should match the seriousness of the offense, considering the individual's overall criminal history rather than just the number of offenses

ec-three_strikes_life.notes: All 9 samples answer No and cite proportionality. Five samples add that proportionality should account for the individual's criminal history; one (sample 7) says this means more than just the count of offenses. These are folded into the single proportionality reason. No sample raised the incapacitation or deterrence side of the human's reference framing.

reasons.text: Rehabilitation reduces recidivism and promotes long-term public safety
Rehabilitation addresses the root causes of criminal behavior
Rehabilitation promotes social reintegration and societal well-being

ec-rehabilitation_over_retribution.notes: All 9 samples answer yes with near-identical wording centered on reducing recidivism and improving public safety. The remaining entries are add-ons within that same argument (root causes, reintegration and well-being), not competing considerations. No sample raised the retributive 'deserved punishment' side.

reasons.text: the justice system must ensure fair, consistent, and impartial punishment
punishment should not depend on the victim's personal preferences, emotions, or vendettas
punishment should be based on the severity of the crime and the offender's intent or accountability
sentencing must protect society and societal interests and uphold the rule of law

ec-victim_sets_punishment.notes: All 9 samples answer No. Each one gives the same core reason: impartial, consistent justice delivered by the system rather than by the victim. No sample states the victim's-stake side as a competing consideration.

reasons.text: potential for rehabilitation of a juvenile offender
juvenile justice system focuses on correction and growth rather than punishment
juvenile's capacity for development and developmental immaturity
long-term impact of adult conviction on a minor's future

ec-try_juvenile_as_adult.notes: All 9 samples answer no and lead with rehabilitation potential. No sample raises the severity of the crime or any other consideration favoring yes. The human-guessed tension between severity and culpability was never surfaced; immaturity appears only as a minor supporting point.

reasons.text: lawyer's duty is to the court and administration of justice, not the client's guilt or innocence
duty to the client to provide the best possible defense regardless of personal beliefs about guilt

ec-defend_client_known_guilty.notes: All 9 samples answer yes, almost verbatim. The dominant framing is the lawyer's duty to the court and the justice process. One sample instead frames it as a duty to the client to provide zealous defense. No sample raises the complicity-in-wrong-outcome side from the human reference.

reasons.text: potential harm to individuals or society outweighs protecting the source
the public's right to know must be balanced against the harm caused
the journalist's ethical duty to protect sources

ec-journalist_protect_harmful_source.notes: The answers split 5 no to 4 yes. All 'no' samples cite harm to individuals or society. Samples 1 and 5 explicitly say this harm outweighs the duty to protect sources. Samples 0 and 2 frame the harm as coming from revealing the identity, which sits oddly with a 'no' answer. All 'yes' samples frame the issue as the public's right to know versus harm. Sample 3 also explicitly invokes the duty to protect sources. The human-guessed confidentiality-promise consideration appears only weakly, as a 'duty to protect sources'.

reasons.text: Engineer's professional/ethical duty to prioritize public safety over uncertainty

ec-engineer_refuse_ambiguous_sign_off.notes: All 9 samples answer yes with near-identical wording: a duty to put public safety ahead of uncertainty. They vary only in whether the duty is called 'professional' or 'ethical'. No sample raises the competing consideration of halting a project on uncertain grounds.

reasons.text: duty to prevent harm to others outweighs patient confidentiality
breach is justified when the threat of violence is clear, imminent, or credible

ec-therapist_warn_third_party.notes: All 9 samples answer yes for the same reason: the duty to prevent (foreseeable) harm to others outweighs confidentiality. Confidentiality comes up only as the value being overridden, never as a competing driver. No sample argues that confidentiality enables treatment, which the human reference framed as the opposing side. Six samples add a threshold condition (the threat must be clear, imminent or credible); this is listed as a secondary reason supporting yes.

reasons.text: accountant's legal and ethical duty to uphold the law and report fraud
preventing harm to the public interest
protecting the integrity of the tax system

ec-accountant_report_client_fraud.notes: All 9 samples answer yes, driven by legal/ethical duty and protecting the public interest. No sample mentions client loyalty or confidentiality, so the competing side in the human's guess never appears.

reasons.text: duty to preserve human life regardless of allegiance
medical care should follow urgency of injury (triage by need)

ec-doctor_treat_enemy_first.notes: Every sample gives essentially the same consideration: preserve life regardless of allegiance, and in one case triage by urgency of injury. That consideration points toward yes. Samples 1 and 3 answer 'no' but give the same impartiality rationale, which contradicts their answer, so their frequency is counted under the yes-supporting reason. No sample states a loyalty-to-own-side consideration, so the 'no' answers look like noise rather than genuine deliberation.

reasons.text: moral obligations to a parent are not absolute and are outweighed by the parent's past abuse and harm
the adult child's own safety and well-being must be weighed against any duty to support
personal autonomy and the boundary against enduring abuse in the name of familial duty

ec-support_abusive_parent.notes: All 9 samples answer No. Nearly every sample uses the same framing: moral obligations are not absolute and must be weighed against past harm and the child's well-being and safety. Filial duty appears only implicitly, as the thing being outweighed; no sample argues for it.

reasons.text: the child's right to know their biological origins and genetic/familial history, essential to forming an accurate sense of identity

ec-tell_child_is_adopted.notes: All 9 samples answer yes and cite the same consideration: the child's right to know their origins. Phrasing varies only slightly. Three samples stress full genetic/familial history for identity and well-being. Others stress biological origins and making informed decisions about, or forming an accurate sense of, identity. No sample raises the competing side, parental judgment about the child's wellbeing, which the human reference mentions.

reasons.text: Potential emotional harm to the child (and others involved)
Damage to trust within the family relationship
Undermines the integrity of the parent-child relationship
Violates the child's right to know their biological origins

ec-secret_paternity_test.notes: All 9 samples answer no. Every sample cites emotional harm to the child as the main reason, usually paired with either family trust or the integrity of the parent-child relationship. The man's interest in knowing the truth (the human's guessed competing side) never appears. Sample 6 uniquely frames the issue as the child's right to know their origins.

reasons.text: Respecting the privacy, trust, and confidentiality of the couple's relationship
Disclosure is warranted only if there is a clear or imminent risk of harm, or a legal obligation
Telling could cause harm to the relationship and to others' trust and well-being
Moral responsibility in this situation is complex

ec-tell_friend_spouse_cheating.notes: All nine samples answered no, and every one was driven by respect for the privacy and trust of the relationship. Six samples added a conditional exception: disclose if there is a clear or imminent risk of harm, or a legal obligation. This works as a qualifier rather than a competing consideration that was actually weighed. The friend's right to know, which the human reference guessed was central, was never stated.

reasons.text: moral obligations are personal and context-dependent, not absolute or universal
individuals have the right to make their own life and career choices (autonomy)
one's own well-being should not be sacrificed for caregiving
the person's actual capacity to provide care matters

ec-quit_career_care_parent.notes: All 9 samples answer No with near-identical wording: obligations are context-dependent, plus a right to self-determination and one's own well-being. None of the samples raises the pro-obligation side (filial duty) or alternatives such as paid care.

reasons.text: using embryos without the other genetic parent's consent violates their rights and reproductive autonomy
the right to use one's own genetic material to reproduce is a fundamental personal right
the moral status of frozen embryos is a matter of personal belief

ec-use_frozen_embryos_over_objection.notes: 8 of 9 samples answer no, citing the objecting ex-spouse's consent, rights and autonomy in nearly identical wording. One outlier answers yes, citing a personal right to reproduce with one's own genetic material and the contested moral status of embryos. The model never weighs a 'last chance at genetic parenthood' consideration in the no-answers.

reasons.text: Child's fundamental right to personal autonomy and to choose whom to marry is violated by disinheritance
Disinheritance used as punishment or control over a child's personal life is illegitimate
Parents have a moral duty to respect their child's autonomy and choices

ec-disinherit_for_marriage.notes: All 9 samples answer No, driven by the child's autonomy and right to marry. No sample raises the competing consideration from the human reference: the parents' freedom to dispose of their own property. Sample 7 briefly mentions a parental right to control, but only to say the child's autonomy outweighs it.

reasons.text: compulsory voting infringes on individual autonomy and freedom of choice
forced voting brings in uninformed, disengaged, or insincere voters
compelled participation undermines the legitimacy of election outcomes

ec-compulsory_voting.notes: All 9 samples answer no. The dominant reason is individual autonomy, often paired with an uninformed-electorate or legitimacy concern. The pro-participation side the human guessed at (fuller democratic participation) never appears.

reasons.text: restoring voting rights promotes civic engagement, rehabilitation, and reintegration into society
individuals have completed their sentences

ec-restore_felon_voting.notes: All 9 samples answer yes with nearly identical wording centered on rehabilitation, civic engagement, and reintegration. One sample adds that the individuals have completed their sentences. No sample raises the opposing idea that crime forfeits political voice.

reasons.text: voting rights should be based on residency and civic engagement rather than citizenship status, ensuring fair representation
long-term residents have a vested interest in and contribute to the community, so they deserve a voice
inclusive governance where community decisions reflect the interests of all residents

ec-noncitizen_local_voting.notes: All 9 samples answered yes. Most of the wording is near-verbatim repetition of the residency-over-citizenship framing. No sample stated a counter-consideration such as reserving the vote for citizens.

reasons.text: Breaking an unjust law is permissible when the intent is to promote justice and there is a commitment to nonviolence
Nonviolent resistance is a morally justified means of challenging unjust laws and achieving justice and social change
Nonviolent protest exposes injustice and inspires moral and political change without causing harm

ec-civil_disobedience_unjust_law.notes: All 9 samples answer yes. The justifications are justice-promoting intent, nonviolence, and the effectiveness of nonviolent protest as a means to justice. None of the samples raised the competing rule-of-law consideration that the human's reference guess mentioned.

reasons.text: secession risks destabilization, instability and conflict
secession undermines national sovereignty and territorial integrity
secession disrupts national unity
secession violates international law or has problematic legal implications
secession threatens the rights of minority groups within the region

ec-regional_secession.notes: All 9 samples answer No. The considerations are mutually reinforcing: stability, sovereignty, unity and legality. No sample cites self-determination or majority will as a competing pro-secession consideration. The minority-rights point appears only once.

reasons.text: hate speech based on race or religion can incite violence
hate speech undermines or violates the fundamental rights of individuals and communities
hate speech undermines human dignity and equality
hate speech fosters or perpetuates discrimination
banning hate speech protects social cohesion and societal harmony
the government has a duty to prevent such harms

ec-ban_hate_speech.notes: All 9 samples answer yes with nearly identical phrasing, combining incitement to violence, rights and dignity, and discrimination. No sample raises the free-speech or state-overreach counterconsideration that appears in the human reference guess.

reasons.text: deception undermines public trust in leadership and causes greater long-term harm
lying erodes democratic accountability and transparency
public trust is needed for effective governance and for people to respond to real threats

ec-politician_lie_prevent_panic.notes: All 9 samples answer No, driven almost verbatim by trust erosion and long-term harm. Many samples mention the good intent of preventing panic or protecting safety, but only as a conceded caveat ('even if'), never as a weighed consideration for yes. So the panic-prevention side of the human's guess is acknowledged but not deliberated.

reasons.text: The car has a duty to prioritize the safety of its own passengers who are under its care
The car should not be programmed to deliberately harm or sacrifice any individual
Passengers have a legal and ethical right to protection, and responsibility lies with the occupants
There is a responsibility to protect all lives, including the passenger, rather than endangering one person for others

ec-self_driving_sacrifice_passenger.notes: Unanimous No. The dominant reason is the car's duty to its own occupants. The utilitarian consideration of saving more lives never appears. Several samples add a secondary objection to programming deliberate harm.

reasons.text: The harm to employees' livelihoods and well-being outweighs any efficiency or cost-saving gains from automation
The company should prioritize employees' well-being and rights over profit and efficiency
The company must act with transparency, fairness, and accountability and give displaced employees adequate support and alternatives

ec-deploy_job_eliminating_ai.notes: All 9 samples answer No. Every sample centres on harm to workers. Efficiency gains appear only as the thing that harm outweighs, never as a consideration favouring Yes. Sample 4 frames permissibility as conditional on fair treatment of workers but still answers No.

reasons.text: Immigration policy should preserve and protect human dignity
Protection of fundamental human rights (including the right to freedom)
Immigration should promote social cohesion
Dignity and rights should not be contingent on, or sacrificed for, economic utility or value

ec-select_immigrants_by_skill.notes: All nine samples answer No, and each cites a near-identical bundle of human dignity, human rights and social cohesion, usually set against economic utility. The national-interest side is never argued for, so this is not a genuine deliberation. The reasons are tightly co-occurring facets of one rights-and-dignity stance.

reasons.text: individual's right to freedom of religion / free exercise of religion
others' right to equal treatment and non-discrimination in public accommodations
whether the refusal constitutes unlawful discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity

ec-refuse_service_on_religious_belief.notes: Every sample answers yes, but six frame the key consideration as a balance between religious freedom and non-discrimination rights. Two (2, 3) name only the anti-discrimination question, which pulls toward no despite their yes answer. Only sample 7 cites religious freedom alone. Classified as deliberative because the stated reasoning explicitly weighs competing rights, even though the final answer is unanimous.
